segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. I am the moderator for this session, which I would retitle as From Vision to Reality. My name is Dr. Francesca Giovannini.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I am teaching at the Harvard Kennedy School. I am also the director of a large nuclear research program at the Belfer Center. And in December last year, I joined as a member of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So I am really, really grateful to be here and to have the chance to shape, together with all of you, this important discussion. Now you have already heard the case for nuclear energy for Africa. And I think this is not the topic for this discussion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But it is instead about how do we get, actually, that vision into reality? What are the things that we need to do on the legal side, on the regulatory side, on the institutional side, in order for nuclear energy projects to come to life in the African continent? Now if I were a policymaker, I would actually be completely overwhelmed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I've heard so many complex ideas, so many challenges, so many obstacles. And so I would like to hear from the experts. What are the lessons learned, the best practices from other countries around the world that have been able to successfully introduce nuclear energy in their countries? And so this panel today, I want to alert you all, is going to be interactive.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now I have some questions for our experts, but I also hope that you will help me, if we have time, with a couple of questions from the audience, just really to drill on what it is that we need to do in order really to bring nuclear energy into reality in the African continent? We want to be pragmatic, we want to be practical, and we actually want to be realistic. Now before I introduce my fantastic panel, I would like you all to turn to the screen, because we have an introductory video.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For governments, strong transactional frameworks help turn national ambition into structured credible projects that capital can evaluate. Liability regimes, insurance, export credit, project contracts, and investor protections are not technical details. They are the foundations of bankability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: This is where legal structure becomes project confidence. Welcome to Legal Advisory and Transactional Frameworks for Nuclear Energy Projects.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Fabulous. Let me introduce my fantastic panel, and I want to underline this is a very rich panel with a lot of different expertise, from international organizations to think tank and national governments, and very rich also because we have on the panel a representative of a country in Africa, in fact Egypt, that has already started building a nuclear power plant. So we have a really living case where we can talk and learn from the case study of Egypt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now let me introduce my fantastic speaker, Christelle Drila, who is the Legislative Assistance Program Lead for the International Atomic Energy Agency. Hen Alcabutli, who is the Senior Associate at Global Nuclear Energy Advisory, who is the advisor now to the Egyptian government for the construction of the El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant. Ariel Levite, Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and Eriel has been also a senior officer in the Israeli Atomic Energy Commission.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And then last but not least, Justin Friedman, who is a former U.S. senior diplomat. He has negotiated many one-to-three agreements around the world with many countries interested in doing business with the United States, and he is now a founder and senior advisor at Friedman Global Strategies. Please help me in welcoming them to this great panel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I also want to make sure that the young people who are here pay attention, because I might call on you for a question. Okay, so just to be clear, you guys cannot sleep, you are going to listen. All right, I want to start with Justin.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Justin, you have had a long career in negotiating one-to-three agreements all around the world with all aspiring countries. But we know that the road from vision to reality is a long one. And so if I'm a policymaker sitting in a nuclear aspirant country, I might actually be quite overwhelmed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Where do I start? What should I do? So what would you say are the most important prerequisites, some of the assumptions or the principles that people in countries that want nuclear energy need to consider at the beginning of their journey?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Wonderful. There we go. Wonderful.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you very much for the question, and thank you to NEISA for this opportunity to speak to a great audience. I'm delighted to be here, my first time in Rwanda, and I have to say I am deeply impressed by the people of the country and by the wonderful achievements you've made in building advanced infrastructure that makes you very much ready for nuclear. And I think if folks didn't see it yesterday, I started the process that led to yesterday's announcement of a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Rwanda on cooperating on nuclear development, and I'm delighted to see that a company that will be speaking I think later this morning, Holtec, has signed an agreement to start doing feasibility study work or pre-feasibility study work for SMR deployment here in Rwanda. So we have a country that's already moving forward into the feasibility stages of nuclear, but before you get to that stage I have three pieces of advice. The first advice is take your time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Nuclear is a long-term relationship, so get to know your potential partners, because you're going to be essentially married to your vendor and to your vendor country's point of origin for maybe 100 years. Because that's, you know, if it's a large reactor it could be 10 years of construction, if it's an SMR it could be as short as three years of construction once all the prep work is done, but then you've got 60 to 80 years of operational life of the reactor, and then another 10 years for decommissioning. So that's a hundred year relationship.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So take your time, you know, date around a little bit, you know, get to know who your partners are going to be, and then make your decision. You know, the second piece of advice is to know yourself. Know your needs as a, what are your plans for energy development?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What are your forecasts for the market? Where do you want to electrify? Where do you want to focus that investment dollar that you have?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Do you want to focus on delivering to rural communities that are underserved? Do you want to focus on industrial supply? Do you want to develop data centers?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Do you want to power industry? Because the answers to those questions will drive very different solutions and nuclear fits differently into each of those categories. And then the third piece of advice is to know your strengths and weaknesses, because you're going to be flooded with people like me who come to the country and say, I got a reactor I want to sell you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Trust me, it's great, it's perfect for you. So you need to know what you know, but also what you don't know. And if you end up hiring someone like me as a strategic advisor or consultant, and yes, I hope you do hire someone like me or me, but if you do end up hiring, remember that you're the boss.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Make me work for you, not work for myself. And that means manage the process, ask the hard questions, and don't take easy answers for the final answer. So that's how I think the first rules of thumb are for getting from vision to reality.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I want to go to you, because you've done a lot of work in nuclear newcomers countries. You have also seen countries that had great intentions, but actually never materialized that vision. And in fact, if you take Vietnam or Indonesia, at least, you know, just a decade ago, these countries really wanted to go towards nuclear energy investments, but in the end, they never materialized.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So what are some of your reflections about what it takes actually to really bring this vision into reality, building on what Justin's saying? So thank you, Francesca, for that question. I think Justin has begun to lead us in the right direction, so let me try and complement what he said in a couple of ways and answer your question in the process.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I think the first thing to understand are the unique attributes of nuclear power. Nuclear is at one and the same time a culture, a process, an institution, a social contract, and nuclear is a huge source of benefits, but if mishandled, could be a huge source of peril as well. The benefits and the risks are both exceptionally great.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I'm not talking just about nuclear disasters. I'm talking about financial disasters, which was the thing that brought the U.S. nuclear progress to extensive areas. And there were a couple of times in the history of nuclear power where expectations were extremely high and they could not be delivered over time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We see now many of the large vendors still struggling to recover from the inability to build them on time, on budget, and in the process jeopardizing the operators, jeopardizing the utilities, jeopardizing the vendors, and so on. So the first thing is to understand that nuclear is unique—Justin has already highlighted one aspect, which is the long-term commitment that it involves, and it's a long-term commitment with the but also with your population. It's a long-term commitment that has many, many, many levels.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So that's point one that I would make. The second point is there is an incredible reservoir of best practices. Those best practices are represented by some organizations that have some presence here, but not all of those who have presence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You want to learn from those organizations, on the one hand, what are the best practices, and then at the same time customize those for local circumstances. I think Hen will actually give you an example of what a struggle it is even to try and anchor those local requirements against best practices of established vendors in a specific project in an African country. So that's the second thing that I would mention.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The third is we've heard a great deal here about the political process, a political and a regional collaboration, and what I want to highlight here is it's clear that for Africa, given many of the specific objective circumstances, regional cooperation is a key to unlocking nuclear power. But at the same time, the same level of political enthusiasm that we were able to see yesterday with the leaders of Tanzania and Rwanda and Togo and so on, has to have a concrete product. What you want to accomplish through that cooperation, and I can go into details in the next round.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you. Fantastic. Christelle, it is obvious also from yesterday's speeches by the presidents that all roads go through the International Atomic Energy Agency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The World Bank has made very clear that a lot of financing will be in partnership with the IEA, and the International Atomic Energy Agency remains the supreme organization that is indispensable for countries to build the legal frameworks that are needed. Can you reflect a little bit about, so if I'm in Rwanda today, what do I need to know about building the legal framework? What does it even mean?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: How does the International Atomic Energy Agency understand those requirements? Thank you. Thank you very much, Francesca.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I would also like to thank the government of Rwanda and EISA for the invitation and to also share the agency's perspective and experience in supporting member states. Indeed, well, the role of the IEA is important in the sense that we are also the guardians of the international legal instruments, and the international legal instruments are one of the important elements when you are thinking of the legal framework. And I would like to echo what has been just said, is that launching a nuclear power program is a strong and long-term commitment that is made by the state.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And if we think about successfully completing a nuclear power program, you need to establish a strong infrastructure. And in that context, you have to also keep in mind that building a nuclear power program is not done in isolation, that you have some national consideration about developing the nuclear legal framework, but you also have some international consideration that you have to take into account. And going to your question about what are the really important elements when considering the legal framework that will be supporting the nuclear power program, I would think about three important conditions that have to be kept in mind, is that your national legal infrastructure will bring some certainty and predictability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's the first thing. The second element is that your legal framework will support the reduction of the risks, and I'll come back to this point. And the third element is responsibility.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: If you allow me, I'll just come back to these three points and give you some practical examples. When it comes to certainty and stability, the legal framework will provide you with the foundation that will be the anchor of your nuclear power program. And this nuclear legal framework is essential, and if you look at the milestone approach for the establishment of a nuclear infrastructure for nuclear power program, you will see that there is this issue five, which is the legal framework, which actually really includes all the elements that you have to take into consideration.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And what the experience has shown is that all the newcomers, they establish this nuclear comprehensive legislation. And what I mean by comprehensive is that you need to have in place nuclear legislation that addresses safety, security, safeguards, and you need also to have a legislation that is separate or incorporated in the nuclear law that addresses nuclear liability. And in addition to that, you have an environment, a legal environment, that includes many other legislation that you have to take into account.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Taxation law, foreign investment law, urban planning law, all these laws also have a role to play in your program. But all these elements will actually provide you with the certainty and the stability that is required to build this nuclear power program. Also, from an investor's perspective, you need to know what are the licensing steps that will support the implementation of the project, and you will find that in your nuclear legislation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Turning to the second element is the reduction of risk. And here again, that's the key message. It's like you need to have a framework that enables the conduct of these activities and implementation of this program in a safe, secure, and peaceful manner.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So going back to one of the elements that was mentioned yesterday in the session that was talking about the public trust, is that the establishment of an independent regulatory body is key in this context, and it is done through the legislation. So that's one of the key elements you have to take into account. A strong regulatory control is essential to ensure that the activities will be conducted in a safe, secure, and peaceful manner in accordance with international standards.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And finally, responsibility. Responsibility is really something important in the sense that, as I said, the nuclear power program is not done in isolation. You have an international community that is also looking at what the state is doing, neighboring countries looking at what states are doing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And so you have to become, join the community by joining the international legal instruments. And you have to have also at the national level, a mechanism that will ensure that if something happens at the level of the nuclear power plants, like an accident, as it happened in the past, unfortunately, you have adequate mechanism to compensate the victims at the national level, but also potential victims in the neighboring countries. So that's what responsibility is about.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And if I may just use to conclude, what I would like to say is that, again, the decision to go for a nuclear power program is a sovereign decision. However, the states that take this sovereign decision, they have to do it right. And they have the responsibility to do it right towards their own population and towards the neighboring countries and the international community.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Terrific. Wow. You could totally teach these things.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Fantastic. All right. So I want to bring a case study.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I think the message with the case study is, look, you might feel a little bit overwhelmed sitting there thinking, oh my God, how am I going to do all these things? But please know that Africa is not the first continent that introduced nuclear power plant. It is doable.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we have to do it right. We have to do it following very specific types of requirements. But you are not going to reinvent the wheel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It is doable. It has been done. And it is important to learn from countries that are going through the process right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And you have a case. In fact, you have more than one case. You have South Africa.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You have Ghana. But perhaps Egypt certainly is leading in a way in thinking about many of these issues. And you have a privileged position as one of the advisors in this nuclear project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You have also visited the Al-Daba nuclear power plant many times. I think it is really fair to ask the question, can you give us a sense of how Egypt has made certain type of decisions in terms of contract, how you design it? What does it actually mean working with the vendor?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What papers do people sign? So give us really this sort of more granular understanding so that countries that come after can really benefit from your experience. Is it working?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you, Francesca. So I want to add some background to my experience before I answer your question. I am an external legal consultant to the Nuclear Power Plants Authority of Egypt, which is the owner entity of El-Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And for the past seven years, I have been based in Cairo, working from NPPA's office and providing them with legal advice on a daily basis for the project implementation. I've been very, very involved in this project. It's special to me because I'm also Egyptian, so it has a personal tie, but also it's an incredible experience to get to see how nuclear power plants are actually built and what that means from a legal perspective.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So to answer your question, Francesca, the contractual framework for the Egyptian project is we have an intergovernmental agreement. It was signed in 2015 with the Russian Federation. And from that intergovernmental agreement, we have four project contracts.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we have a turnkey EPC contract, we have a contract for the construction of a storage facility for spent fuel on site, we have a contract for the provision of operation support and maintenance, and we have a fuel supply contract. So it's a very comprehensive package for the delivery of the nuclear power plant, but also for post-construction in terms of providing operation support and also providing fuel supply, which is a bit of a unique deal. If I were to talk about a recommended contractual approach for a newcomer country, I think a turnkey EPC contract is highly recommended because in this model, the risk is placed on the party that is best positioned to manage it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And from an engineering perspective, this means you will have an EPC contractor who is responsible for the design, for the construction, for the procurement, and they deliver a nuclear power plant that is ready to be operated. So this extremely minimizes the interface risk for the owner. As a first-time owner, you don't want to be managing subcontractors or managing interfaces between different scopes of supply, or let alone managing interfaces between different project contracts that serve specific purposes within the implementation of a nuclear power plant for the first time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On the other hand, your vendor has experience, they've built nuclear power plants before, they've delivered successful projects, so they are best placed and best positioned to handle this risk. That said, one very important point I want to make here is this does not mean that the owner does not have a role in the project implementation. In fact, the owner has an essential oversight role, even in the context of a turnkey EPC model, where you would think your contractor is going to do everything for you, that is very far from the reality.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the owner's oversight role is critically important, and the first reason is the owner is the licensee, and from that role, there derives an oversight responsibility, especially for nuclear safety. So you have to oversee all aspects of the contractor scope that are being performed, starting from design reviews, overseeing construction works and even supervising the manufacturing activities. So there is also a very critical role for the owner in the context of a turnkey EPC model.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I will come back asking you what the challenges are, because I think you have some very good answers for that. I want to go back to you, Justin, and maybe to reflect a little bit what you heard so far, but mostly from your negotiating standpoint. You have negotiated a lot of one-to-three agreements, and you said to these countries, you are in charge, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So you need to come with an idea of what you want to get out of these negotiations. Can I ask you, what are the things you have heard in your negotiations that are common? So what do countries ask, for example, in the negotiations of the one-to-three agreement?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Or what can they possibly ask when they are in fact approaching the process of a one-to-three agreement? So thank you for the question. I will caveat this, that I have been involved in some of the one-to-three negotiations, but my deeper negotiation is in what we call these intergovernmental agreements, which are about partnering with the United States government to promote the adoption of U.S. technologies in a particular market. But I think the questions are the same. On the one-to-three side, one-to-three agreements, for those who are not familiar with them, are required by U.S. law. That is, before the United States can allow the export of nuclear materials or nuclear technology, we have to have a one-to-three agreement, which gives us assurance.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I am speaking sort of as if I am still in the U.S. government, but I am not. But I am still an American, so forgive me. But it gives us assurance that the materials and the technology will only be used for peaceful purposes, and they will not be re-exported without our permission.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And understanding that negotiation process is very important. And I did work prior to this in the U.S. government on export control assistance. So I helped countries build their structures so that they could enforce controls of sensitive goods and trade in sensitive goods.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So I have seen it from a number of different angles. In a one-to-three, the biggest question is often, what does this allow us to do together? And sometimes there is a desire to make them smaller and tailored and simplified.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, we are only going to build one big reactor, or we are only going to cooperate on a research reactor. Many countries come back and say, well, you know what, today we need a research reactor, tomorrow we think we need a large power reactor, and the day after tomorrow we want to have an SMR or ten SMRs, and the day after that we may want to be involved in the fuel cycle. So the complexities of the negotiation often revolve around, what does this allow, and do we want to have enough flexibility so we don't have to renegotiate every five years?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But the other side is these intergovernmental agreements. And for those, you can guess, obviously we are trying to create an opportunity for U.S. businesses. And the agreements, the important fact to know about these agreements is, they don't mandate the use of any one company's technology, they don't mandate the use of American technology, but they create a platform by which governments can talk to each other to make sure that deals and processes move forward in support of a construction project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Terrific, thank you. Eli, could I bring the regional aspect to this? Because I know you have thought a lot about how regional cooperation in a way helps countries, maybe share also some of the burdens of building all these institutions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can you comment a little bit on how you see the role of regional cooperation in all this? Francesca, for this question. Look, the point of departure ought to be regional cooperation has been something that has been discussed in many regions and implemented successfully only in a handful, and even then was handled for specific purposes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the first question to ask is, what is regional cooperation supposed to achieve? And I'll give you five possibilities of what regional cooperation could achieve. One is to achieve economies of scale, whether it's economies of scale on the grid, on the purchasing power, on the vendor selection, and so on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Particularly acute here in Africa, because when you have a grid that is in like in Rwanda, 430 megawatts at the moment, clearly one nuclear power plant is the most that you could accommodate. But also if every country gets into a different supplier, then it's not actually March sort of capitalizing on your purchasing power. The second is issues of burden sharing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It doesn't make sense for everyone to do the work themselves. You can accomplish sovereignty, but you have to balance it against pragmatism. It doesn't produce for every, it doesn't make sense for every country to produce its own fuel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It doesn't make sense for every country to dispense of the spent fuel or the nuclear waste and so on. It doesn't make sense for every country to develop the entire human capital and to build on a point that some of my predecessors have meant. Do you know what effort it means to actually license a nuclear power plant, particularly if it's a first of a kind?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's an incredibly onerous exercise. It doesn't make sense for every newcomer country to do it by itself. Can you engage the NRC, the French, the Canadians, the Russians, whoever it is, and so on, so you don't absolutely have to do it by yourself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It makes sense to do it regionally. So that's a second. But the burden sharing could range from the human, to the capital, to the physical, and even to the territorial.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The third is to harness the relative advantages. There are some areas which are less suitable for deployment, nuclear power plants, for disposing of nuclear spent fuel and so on. You want to take advantage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Some have more advanced capabilities in certain areas over others. You want to try and do some burden sharing and you want to harness the relative advantages. The fourth is risk management and allocation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You want resilience. If Rwanda were to build a nuclear power plant tomorrow and the plant would for some reason be idle, where would you get the power? The most a grid could currently accommodate is one nuclear power plant.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: If you don't have a resilient system and transmission with a neighboring country, look at the role that France is playing for nuclear energy supply across Europe as an example. So you want this as part of the risk management and so on, but you want it for another reason as well. If you recall what Justin was saying, it's a long-term commitment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Sorry, politicians come and go. You don't want this to be identified with one president or the other president and so on. If you create a regional framework, you anchor this obligation for a much longer time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And finally, if we look at other regions, the role of mutual reassurance has played an incredibly important role between Argentina and Brazil, across the European countries and so on. Reassurance that everyone will get equitable access, reassurance that it will only be used for peaceful purposes and so on. So the first thing about regional collaboration is to understand that doing it at least sub-regionally makes eminent sense, but you should know what you're looking yourself into, harmonize that requirement, and I mention this because I think that the next practical step in this region would be between now and the meeting of UNICEF next year in Togo, is to have a much clearer idea and ideally take the incredibly impressive vision that we have heard yesterday from the presidents of some African countries and try and channel them into a practical understanding of what you want to accomplish regionally, at least initially. I knew he had been thinking quite a lot about regional cooperation, so that's why I raised that question to him. Justin, please.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We get this mic up? There we go. Two quick points.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: One, the point about political stability and the programs will last through several governments. The intergovernmental agreement that I mentioned, the best example of that is the Poland agreement, where it was negotiated under the first Trump administration with the then Polish government, then we had the Biden administration and the work continued, and then the Polish government changed and the work continued, and then Trump was re-elected, and now it's continuing with the Trump and the new Polish government.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So, two different changes of government on both sides, and the projects continue. On the regional cooperation, it is so important because the African market is clear in my mind that it will be huge, but to bring the investors here, to bring the technology providers here, they need to see that they're not going to have to reinvent the reactor for every market, and that's one of the advantages of SMRs is that they will be coming out of a factory and they'll be very consistent. And so, if you cooperate now on a general set that harmonizes your regulations, the vendors will know, okay, I'll sell my first in Rwanda, I'll sell my second in Tanzania, my third in Togo, my fourth in Rwanda, my fifth in another market, but it'll be the same reactor.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And so, for them, the costs go down, and that means for the customer, the costs go down. So, regional cooperation is not just a nice thing to talk about, it's about money and it's about attracting investment and technology. Awesome.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I want to build on what you say and ask Christelle about nuclear liability in particular. Now, let me say that all the things we are saying today are not only a requirement to make this investment safe, they're also necessary to make the market accessible to these investors, because investors will not come in a country that doesn't have a strong regulatory framework. And so, it is also a way to open up the country for investment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Nuclear liability is a political issue, or has become a political issue, because, of course, investors look at who actually gets, ultimately, the blame if something goes wrong. That's how I put it. Christelle, you can challenge that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Tell us a little bit more about nuclear liability and how important it is to give investors confidence. Thank you very much. I would try to be very concise on liability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We could talk for hours about that, but let me put it in a simple way. The nuclear liability regime is a regime that is established to provide adequate compensation to victims in case a nuclear accident happens at a nuclear installation, let's make it simple, at a nuclear power plant, or during the course of transport of nuclear material to or from that nuclear power plant. And as history has shown, if something happens at a nuclear power plant, it will actually trigger large-scale damages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We have seen the accident of Chernobyl. We have seen what happened in Fukushima. Earlier on, there were three mile lands, although there were no transboundary consequences at this stage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But the potential of transboundary consequences are very important. And one of the things that the regime does is actually to provide specific rules to manage transboundary claims in case of a nuclear accident. So that's what the regime does.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And in this context, and that comes back to your question, is that we have a number of international instruments that have been developed to address this question of nuclear liability regime. Fortunately, I would say they are all based on seven key liability principles. And I will not go into these details here, but the idea is to make sure that there is a channeling of the liability to one entity, the operator.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is an amount of compensation that is available to the victims. We have identified in advance the type of damage that would be covered, etc. So we have this channeling of the liability, the channeling of the jurisdiction, which aims to actually facilitate the compensation and provide adequate compensation to the victims.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: At the same time, it goes back to also providing legal certainty for the vendors and the supplier countries. Because if something happens, and if you had to apply general tort law, you would have multiple claims in multiple countries, and it would trigger a large litigation procedure. And that's really something that is possibly to the detriment of the victims.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So that's why we have this regime in place. Now, there are some challenges coming with that. As I said, we have multiple instruments that are existing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We have instruments that historically have been developed in OECD countries, the Paris Convention on Third-Party Liability for Nuclear Damage, that is mostly gathering countries in Europe. And we have a regime for civil liability that has been developed in Vienna, the Vienna Convention on Civil Liability. So that was in the early days of the development of the nuclear industry in the 60s.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And then Chernobyl happens. And this, it was realized by the international community that there was a need to strengthen, to provide better rules to adequately protect the victims. So these conventions have been revised and enhanced to provide more compensation to more victims, to more types of damages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we have a revised liability regime. We have a revised Vienna regime. And on top of this, we had to address the specific case of the United States that could not join any of these conventions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we have the Convention on Supplementary Compensation, which aims to provide a global nuclear liability regime that can be joined by all states in the world that are developing, operating a nuclear power plant, or contemplating to do so. So basically, for a state, can you imagine a state embarking on a nuclear power program? They have all these instruments in front of them, and they are facing this difficulty, which one shall I join?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And that brings me to the second element. We were talking about the investment and knowing what we know and what we don't know. And when it comes to nuclear liability, it is a very specific expertise, and we don't have too many people at the national level that are knowledgeable about this topic.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So building some knowledge and capabilities for these countries to understand what liability means, and to make a knowledgeable decision about which instrument shall I join, noting that some countries have joined all of these instruments, where some others have chosen one or two of them. And that depends on many factors, which also render the thing even more complicated. The first one could be, who are your vendor countries?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Because the idea of this regime is to be in treaty relations with other states. So you are building this treaty relation, and the first treaty relation, of course, you want to build is with your vendor country, because you also want the supply state to be in treaty relation with you, and vice versa, and the same with the supplier. So that's one thing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But you have some other regional consideration. We talk about, you look at your neighboring countries. We are in Rwanda here, and you are looking, you have also several neighboring countries that are considering going nuclear power.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: If they join, if they are building a nuclear power plant, you want to make sure that you are in treaty relation with these neighboring countries, to have adequate compensation in case something happens in this neighboring country. So you have to think about that. And then another thing, if I may even complicate the picture, it depends also on your geographical position.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: If you are a coastal state, you have the issue of transport of nuclear material, and if you are likely to be affected by transport, maybe you want to be in treaty relations with these countries that are transporting. So all of this is one of the elements, and probably one of the things that countries have to think about, and to make sure that whatever convention they are becoming party to, it is adequately reflected at the national level. Because when actually you will be negotiating the contracts with a vendor country, the first thing they will look at in your national nuclear legislation is the liability provisions that you have, to make sure that actually the allocation of the risk is clear, and the principle of liability are clearly reflected.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So, and this is again an exercise that is not easy, and for which of course the IEA is providing support, but we'll come back to that later. Thank you. Perfect.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Eli, you have a point on this, and then I go to Ant. So just to make it clear, because I think the discussion could be legal, but the discussion could also be political, and ought to be political. So just to illustrate three things.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Number one, the liability regime is an incredibly important element of the social contract between the government and the people. We have multiple bad examples in this space. India, because of the kind of liability laws they put in place, stopped the ability to get nuclear power plants for many years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The Japanese went into Fukushima with a problematic liability regime. So that's one. It's a critical aspect of the social contract.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Point number two, it has already been explained that the liability treaties of different kinds cover both level of compensation and scope of compensation, which is different. We need to make clear that, for example, is just the damages include environmental remediation, or just direct damages, to give you an example of why this is a political choice that has to be modified, then incorporated in the legal aspect. And finally, just to say, we have recently found that nuclear power plants could end up unintentionally in war zones.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That has happened in Ukraine. That has happened in the UAE. That has happened in Iran.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The liability conventions are highly, all of them are highly deficient in dealing with this scenario. So we need to understand that there are, again, political issues that need to be worked upon. And so when you develop your own liability regime, you can build on the international institutions, but you have to add to that a local component.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I want you to reflect on all this, bring it back to Egypt, and also tell us a little bit from your standpoint. I mean, we are hearing a lot of things that need to be done. I'm sure you have some experiences also on challenges that you are to face.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Good luck. I wanted to shed some light on nuclear liability from a contractual perspective and also from a practical perspective. I feel like, like Christelle, I'm also very passionate about nuclear liability, personally, because it's very unique to the nuclear industry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It has principles that apply only to nuclear, and they're very complicated. So as Christelle said, the first thing I want to say is it's very important to make sure that you have a comprehensive nuclear liability regime. And this, of course, comes from joining international conventions on nuclear liability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There are a couple of them, and each one or all of them could be relevant depending on the specific circumstances of the member state that is considering building this aspect of the regulatory framework. But having a comprehensive nuclear liability regime by joining the conventions and also transferring it to your national law, whether in the form of a separate nuclear liability law, only governing this matter, or having a comprehensive nuclear liability law that covers everything, including nuclear liability, is very important from a contractual perspective, because then it allows you to use this as a basis to draft your nuclear liability clause. And as Christelle mentioned, this is one of the key provisions in any contracts for the construction of a nuclear power plant. And from a practical perspective also, vendors and suppliers have their own requirements for nuclear liability provisions when they are considering being involved in a specific project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And if you don't have that comprehensive framework, starting from the treaties, the national law, and then the contractual provision, you will be exposed to having to address individual requests from each supplier on what they need to be able to participate in the project, and it's really far from ideal. The best approach is to have a comprehensive regime that you apply to everyone that is seeking to be involved in your project. And of course, this brings us back to which convention.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Well, I think personally, in my view, the best approach is join as many of them so that you can have the best coverage possible. And this saves you the agony of having to address individual requests from individual suppliers and vendors, depending on where they come from. Because regardless of the vendor that you will supply at the end, you will have companies involved from all over the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And this is very common in nuclear projects. So it's a good practice to join as many conventions and have as much coverage as possible. Terrific.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: All right. I have one last question, but I do want maybe to have a couple of questions from the floor. I see several representatives, Kenya and Ghana.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'm sure many of you are already thinking along those lines. I have a question for three of you, but a different one from Kristal. And Justin, I want to start with you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In a conversation with Hend, she actually noted one of the biggest challenges is, you know, you are a country in a rush. You want to get the energy. You need that energy, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But at the same time, you have to build your regulatory framework. And you also need to look at the vendors and what's out there. And this process needs to go in parallel, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Because if I'm waiting to do the first one and then the other, it's going to take me 25 years. So how does one think about this, right? I have to make regulatory decisions before I even have a concert with the vendor.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So it's a little bit of catch-22. How would you recommend countries to think about this? So you are asking the countries that are newcomers to, as we say, walk and chew gum at the same time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And most of us can do that. So the first advice is take a deep breath. And then say, yes, let's do it step by step in an orderly fashion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I would recommend that as you think about nuclear and want to go through these processes, you look, of course, of course, to the IAEA milestones process. Because that is the standard about how to move through the 19 questions that you have to answer as you get ready for a nuclear program. Now, I only took off my U.S. government hat eight months ago. So I'm going to advertise a U.S. government program, because I think it's a great program. And it's called FIRST. And if you were at the plenary yesterday, you heard Renee Sonderman mention it as well. What FIRST does here in Africa and around the world is bring together professionals to talk about and talk through these very questions and share best practices and bring in maybe even some of the people on the panel today to be expert speakers to help you understand the challenges and then make good decisions as they work best for your country.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So seek out that international support. And then, of course, taking off my ex-U.S. government hat and putting on my consulting hat, look at someone like me who can be your partner, not to tell you what to do, but to be your partner to ask good questions, to help you make sure that you're not missing something along the way, and take that journey together with someone like me. And I'm sounding like my wife right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: My wife is a professional coach. And so she talks about asking good questions and journey together. But that is true.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You need a partner in this journey. And so seek out someone like me or someone else to make this journey possible. Terrific.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Eli, can you help us think through this Catch-22 problem and maybe how international partnership can help also? So we talked about a long period of incubation. And the long period of incubation manifests itself in the contract negotiations and so on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But I think earlier when we talked about understanding the issues and understanding how the various vendors are coming at it from different directions is an extremely important part. So I would say the following. Look, in my judgment, there are three stages where you need external help.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is the incubation stage where I think some of the consultants that you've heard around the table, and this is giving an example and so on, are extremely important. Not many of them, but a handful of them in each area to identify for you the questions, to identify for you the options, to show you what are the implications of choice between those options, and to leave the choice to you. So they both, you should know where to use them, but not where to use them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So that's phase one. Phase two, as you get closer to operations, I think we need to think of the ones who are representing not just the kind of the milestones, but actually representing the best practices of running nuclear power plants. And then we need to think of the World Association of Nuclear Operators.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We need to think of World Institute of Nuclear Security and the role that they could help you that you don't have to reinvent the wheel and so on. And the third part, which can be in between, but hasn't been mentioned thus far, and I think worryingly so, the financial institutions want to know that you're meeting the requirements that minimize their risk. If you don't have auditing functions that can attest to the fact that those boxes are being checked, you will not get a penny from them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And the IEA is not an auditing institution. It's a political institution. It has a lot of professional expertise, which is invaluable, but it's not an auditing function for multiple reasons.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the question you have to ask yourself is, who can ascertain that I meet those requirements across the various areas and so on in a way that is transparent to the ones who are supposed to fund it? And here you have to understand, we're talking about government ministries, not just the one in charge of nuclear energy, but it could be the Ministry of the Treasury, the Financial Responsibility Agency, it could be the Ministry of Energy more broadly, and so on. So they need to know that their commitment, that the commitment you have undertaken will indeed provide you with a reliable, safe, sustainable nuclear power.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the auditing function is so. So what I'm basically trying to get across is, the points of reference vary over time and vary over function. Awesome.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Christelle, let me bring you in and then I give a hand to the final word on Egypt. How does the IEA help in all this? Give us some examples of your work and how the IEA works on these really complex issues.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you very much for that. But maybe before addressing this point directly, I just wanted to come back to this issue of the phased approach. And I would like to highlight that, of course, the IEA, as it was mentioned, we don't act as an inspector as such, except in the area of safeguards, where we have specific roles and functions that are mandated to the IEA.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But for the other area, we are supporting, we are providing guidance to member states. And in this context, I would really like to highlight that the milestone approach that has been developed by the agency, the milestone approach, it's a document that really helps the state and accompanies the states in developing the required infrastructure, supporting the nuclear power program. And this milestone approach will actually guide states in identifying what needs to be done and when it needs to be done.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And it has this phased approach from phase one, phase two, to phase three. And you have probably heard that in many countries we have, they have conducted this in-ear mission, which will actually help the countries to assess where they are at this phase one, where actually they are taking the way and they are at the end of phase one, they are considered as ready to make a knowledgeable decision to go for nuclear. Then you have phase two, where it's the contracting elements and they are negotiating the contract.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And at the end of phase two, they are ready to sign the contract. And phase three is the operation. And when it comes to the legal, what we are expecting, we have also this phased approach.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And it is expected that at the end of phase one, when the state makes this decision to go for nuclear, the state should have a clear understanding of the instrument they need to join. And they need to have also a clear understanding of what are the elements they need to have in the legislation. And at the end of phase two, when they are ready at the stage where they are of the contract bidding and contract, this is where it is expected that they are ready to party to a number of international instruments.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And they are, they have already enacted a nuclear legislation that have these elements that we briefly touched upon earlier in this discussion. Now, coming to your question, how we help, and I will focus here on the support that is provided in the Office of Legal Affairs and in particular in the Nuclear and Treaty Law section with this program that I am leading, which is the Legislative Assistance Program. And we have a comprehensive and ready multifaceted tool, which starts at the very early stage of the development of the legislation until this finalization.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And again, I would like to go back to this issue of the time frame. All of this needs to be built in the long term. Developing nuclear legislation takes time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Enacting a nuclear legislation takes time. We have examples of countries that took more than 10 years to actually finally enact legislation. And then it's about investing in your people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That was something that was mentioned. And building the capacity at the national level to have nuclear lawyers that will be supporting the implementation of the nuclear power program from the regulator's perspective, from the industry perspective is also key. And it takes time again.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So on all these factors, the agency is providing support. We are conducting workshops in member states, helping member states to identify what are the key elements that they need to have in their national legislation. And it's really a tailored approach.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Here we are in the context of a nuclear power program. So it's a comprehensive legislation that would address nuclear safety, nuclear liability, transport, waste management. We talked about the long-term commitment for the management of the waste, which is an important element in establishing a regulatory body.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But we also have some countries that do not have all these considerations. They have few resources to manage, few resources at the national level, and we are crafting the help to support their needs to develop legislation adapted to their needs. So that's one thing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Then we have this very concrete work. We are receiving draft legislation and we are working on the draft legislation, providing comments, suggestions, working with the drafting team in the country, in the IEA. So that's really something concrete and we are doing that over the years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We have back and forth between the country and the IEA doing that. And another important element is that once you have a text that is pretty mature, integrates the international legal instruments requirements, and responds to the needs of the country, you have to make sure that the legislature will follow you and finally the law will be adopted. So we also have this conversation with decision and policy makers, with parliamentarians, and this is something we are doing more and more within the Office of Legal Affairs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We are talking with the parliamentarians to explain what is a nuclear legislation, how it will support your project to develop a nuclear power program, and why all these elements are critical to have in the national legislation. And usually it helps and supports the enactment of the legislation. And finally, last but not least, capacity building, as I was mentioning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And on that we have developed over the years different training programs. Our flagship program is the Nuclear Law Institute, which is a two-week training program really focusing on the drafting of legislation. But we are also organizing workshops in member states.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The idea is really to transfer knowledge to the people and make sure that then it's like a chain, that knowledge is transferred at the national level. So we are trying to really build this chain of knowledge to make sure that these states have the capabilities. Making a knowledgeable decision means also understanding what you are talking about and having the competence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So that's what we are doing in the Office of Legal Affairs. Thank you. Terrific.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Handa, I want to finish with you. You've heard all this conversation. Egypt is really in the thick of the process now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Just reflect a little bit about lessons learned from your experience, what you've seen, what newcomers need to know from your experience in designing all these legislations to build the legal framework, to build the capacities. And just draw a little bit of maybe best practices and lessons learned from some of these countries. Thank you, Francesca.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The first lesson I learned I wanted to share was about nuclear liability, but I think we've covered that sufficiently. Another lesson learned I think is very important, and Christelle also talked about this, is capacity building. And I know a lot of people talk about this, but it is a very important topic that really deserves being talked about separately.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I will talk from the perspective of the owner, and building the institutional capacity of the owner is extremely important. One first reason for that is, as I mentioned, the owner will have a critical role in the management of the project and oversight over the contractor's performance. But the other thing is, when we say capacity building, the first thing that comes to mind is technical knowledge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the engineers, their experience with nuclear technology, how their reactors are built, how they're delivered. But it's also very important to invest in their legal knowledge. So the legal knowledge of the future operator and the owner entity, in terms of familiarizing them with all of the principles that are so unique to the nuclear industry, most of them coming from international conventions, and also with the provisions of their contracts, so that they're aware of their obligations, their risks, their requirements based on the contracts, and this is very important.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I guess another lesson learned that I can share is ensuring that you have a clarity of roles in your project contracts. You don't want to have uncertainties about who's responsible for a certain scope or who's responsible for a certain obligation. You want to map out these obligations as clearly as possible because I think there are no perfect contracts in the world, and even if you have a very good contract, experience shows that when you start to implement it practically, there will be different positions on how you interpret them, there will be issues and there will be disagreements that you will have to resolve.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So just a very good practice is to try to draft the contract in a manner that is as clear as possible, make sure each party's responsibilities are clear, each one is the risk allocation is clear, so that you can minimize this uncertainty that will arise at some point from the practical application. All right, I will give you 30 seconds. So I would be remiss if we didn't mention that one of the co-sponsors of this conference is the Nuclear Energy Agency of the OECD.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They are a huge depository of knowledge of the best practices across the nuclear disciplines, and now that they're not only looking at the OECD countries and collaborating in some form with both China and Russia, but also extending a hand to the developing world that wants to get into nuclear, you would be mistaken if you don't tap their extended hand to actually get into the nuclear law issues and learn them, and so on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So rather than just going to individual experts, you could rely heavily on the Nuclear Energy Agency to help guide you, including an international law conference and things of that nature, and then school and whatever. So the Nuclear Energy Agency, I think, is a huge asset out there that you want to tap. So Christelle, Hent, Ellie, Justin, I really want to thank you for a very rich conversation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: To those of you who are in the audience, I'm sorry I couldn't take your question, but these experts are going to be around. Please make sure that if you have questions, if you want to know more about their expertise, you just reach out to them at the end of the session. And again, thank you so much for this terrific discussion.
